approachQuestion.prompt:
Batch sizing

Given two nonnegative integer batch sizes a and b, return their greatest common divisor: the largest nonnegative integer that divides both. Define gcd(0,0)=0. Return one integer and do not modify the inputs.

Example 1: a=84, b=30 -> 6.
Example 2: a=0, b=27 -> 27.
Example 3: a=0, b=0 -> 0.
constraints: Inputs and intermediate integer values are exact signed 64-bit integers.
Return gcd(0,0)=0. The output is one integer.

options.text: Set a to the larger value and b to the smaller. Repeatedly replace (a,b) with (b, a mod b) until b is zero, then return a.
options.feedback: Each remainder step preserves the common divisors while reducing the second value.

options.text: Set a to the larger value and b to the smaller. While they differ, subtract the smaller from the larger; return their common value.
options.feedback: This is correct for all nonnegative inputs and preserves the common divisors, but repeated subtraction can make very small progress when the values are far apart.

options.text: Try every positive integer up to the smaller input and keep the largest candidate that divides both values.
options.feedback: This finds the answer, but checks many candidates individually even though common divisors can be preserved through a smaller pair.

options.text: Return the absolute difference of the two inputs, treating zero difference as the answer.
options.feedback: A difference need not be the greatest common divisor: for (18, 12), the difference is 6 and the greatest common divisor is also 6, but for (20, 12) the difference 8 is not a common divisor; the correct answer is 4.

feedback.reason: Replacing (a,b) by (b,a mod b) preserves their common divisors.
details: For a pair (a,b), write a as a multiple of b plus a remainder. A number divides both a and b exactly when it divides b and that remainder. Replace the pair with (b, remainder) and repeat until the second value is zero; the first is the greatest common divisor. If both inputs are zero, return zero by the stated convention.

Replacing (a,b) by (b,a mod b) preserves their common divisors. Stop at second value zero; the first is the greatest divisor. The task explicitly defines gcd(0,0)=0 instead of requiring a positive divisor there.

“Set a to the larger value and b to the smaller. Repeatedly replace (a,b) with (b, a mod b) until b is zero, then return a.”: Each remainder step preserves the common divisors while reducing the second value.

“Set a to the larger value and b to the smaller. While they differ, subtract the smaller from the larger; return their common value.”: This is correct for all nonnegative inputs and preserves the common divisors, but repeated subtraction can make very small progress when the values are far apart.

“Try every positive integer up to the smaller input and keep the largest candidate that divides both values.”: This finds the answer, but checks many candidates individually even though common divisors can be preserved through a smaller pair.

“Return the absolute difference of the two inputs, treating zero difference as the answer.”: A difference need not be the greatest common divisor: for (18, 12), the difference is 6 and the greatest common divisor is also 6, but for (20, 12) the difference 8 is not a common divisor; the correct answer is 4.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed remainder-reduction method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let m be the smaller input.
constraints: Auxiliary space includes temporary state and the call stack, but excludes supplied input and returned output.

options.text: O(log m) time, O(log m) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Euclidean remainder reduction uses logarithmically many steps and fixed scalar state.
details: Remainders shrink geometrically over pairs of steps, while the iterative method retains a fixed number of integers.

For m=0 the method returns immediately. For positive inputs, each two consecutive remainder steps reduce the positive remainder by at least a constant factor; the number of steps is logarithmic in m. The worst case is attained up to constant factors by consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
The iterative method retains only two integer variables and a temporary remainder. It uses no recursion stack or size-dependent structure.

Inputs are nonnegative integers up to 10^18 and are represented exactly in signed 64-bit integers. Remainders stay within the input range; the algorithm performs no multiplication or addition that can overflow. This is a fixed-width integer model, not arbitrary-precision arithmetic.
Iterative Euclidean reduction; fixed number of signed 64-bit words, no recursion. Input and scalar output are excluded.
